Not long ago I was staying in a village where the shortest cut to the inn lay through the churchyard, and passing and repassing so often I came to know the dead inhabitants of the place almost better than the living. Not with the penetrating knowledge of the author of "Spoon River Anthology"—that very extraordinary and understanding book,—but in a kindly superficial way. Indeed, considering that they were total strangers and their acquaintance not now to be made by any but the followers of those doughty knights of the round (or square) séance table, Sir Oliver and Sir Conan, some of these dead people were absurdly often in my thoughts; but that was because of their names. Such names! Many of course were no longer legible, for Father Time had either obliterated them with his patient finger, dipped now in lichen and now in moss, or upon them his tears had fallen too steadily. But many remained and some of them were wonderful. Has it ever been explained why the dead have more remarkable names than the living? Did any one ever meet "in the form" a Lavender Wiseways? Yet there was a Lavender Wiseways lying beneath one of those stones. There was her sister too, lying close beside—Lavinia Wiseways. Neither had married; but then how could they have performed a deed which would have lost them such distinction! And who now exchanges market greetings, with a gaitered gentleman named Paradine Ebb? Yet once there was a Paradine Ebb, farmer, not such a great distance from London, to shake by the hand, and chat to, and buy fat stock from, and, I hope, share a cordial glass with. And who—but if I continue I shall betray the village's name, and that is against good manners. Too many real names get into print in these inquisitive days.

message.content: During a recent stay in a quaint village, I found that the quickest route to the inn took me through the churchyard. As I walked this path repeatedly, I became familiar with the deceased residents of the area, perhaps even more so than with the living. My understanding was not as deep as that of the author of "Spoon River Anthology," who possesses an exceptional and insightful grasp of the dead, but rather a light-hearted acquaintance. It struck me as amusing that, given these individuals were complete strangers to me and could only be known through the efforts of those brave seekers of the supernatural, like Sir Oliver and Sir Conan, they occupied my thoughts quite frequently. This was largely due to the peculiar names I encountered. Many names had faded beyond recognition, eroded by the relentless passage of time, their inscriptions blurred by layers of lichen and moss or worn away by the tears of ages. However, some names remained intact and were truly remarkable. Have we ever pondered why the deceased often bear such extraordinary names compared to the living? Who among us has ever met a Lavender Wiseways in real life? Yet beneath one of those stones lay a Lavender Wiseways. Her sister, Lavinia Wiseways, rested nearby. Neither of them had wed, but it seems they could hardly give up such unique identities. And who now greets a gentleman in gaiters named Paradine Ebb? Once, not far from London, there was a farmer named Paradine Ebb, with whom one could exchange handshakes, converse, and perhaps enjoy a drink. Yet, I must be cautious not to reveal the village's name, as it would be impolite to disclose too many real names in today's inquisitive society.
